title: The genetic code: DNA, chromosomes and genes
specPoints: Year 9 bridging: chromosomes, DNA, genes, base pairing, variation and its two kinds

tips.title: Cell, nucleus, chromosome, DNA, gene
tips.body: Big to small, and a gene is *part of* a chromosome, never the other way round. A human body cell has **46** chromosomes in **23 pairs**; a gamete has **23**. If you remember the pairs, the gamete number follows: one of each pair.

tips.title: The pairs are equal, and the four add to 100
tips.body: For a base-percentage question: A = T and C = G. Write down the one you are given, copy it to its partner, subtract both from 100, and halve what is left for the other pair. Then add all four; if they do not make 100, something is wrong.

tips.title: Groups or a range?
tips.body: If the characteristic comes in a few **named groups** with nothing between, it is **discontinuous**: bar chart with gaps, usually one gene. If it can take **any value** and needs measuring, it is **continuous**: grouped into equal ranges, one bar each, many genes plus environment.

tips.title: Franklin took the picture, Watson and Crick built the model
tips.body: Four names, two jobs. **Franklin** and **Wilkins** made the **X-ray photographs** in London; **Watson** and **Crick** built the **model** in Cambridge in **1953**. The Nobel Prize in 1962 could not include Franklin, who had died in 1958.

tips.title: Inherited, environmental, or both
tips.body: Ask two questions: *could you be born with it?* and *could life change it?* Yes and no: inherited (blood group). No and yes: environmental (a scar). Yes and yes: both (height). Most interesting characteristics are both, and saying so is usually the stronger answer.

why.matters: Every cell you have carries the same set of instructions, written in a four-letter alphabet along molecules you cannot see, and copied without error billions of times since you were one cell. That is the fact behind inheritance, behind why you look like your parents and unlike your brother, behind ancestry tests, twins, blood groups and the diseases that run in families. The GCSE Genetics unit works out the rules of inheritance and how a gene becomes a protein; this topic gives it the objects to work with, from chromosome to base, and the two kinds of variation those objects produce.

examples.title: The ancestry test
examples.body: Spit in a tube, and a few weeks later a company tells you a quarter of your DNA comes from one part of the world. The quarter is a grandparent. You inherited half your chromosomes from each parent, one of every pair, and each parent had inherited half of theirs from each of their parents. So a grandparent's share is half of a half, and a great-grandparent's is half again. The test is reading the same halving that makes brothers and sisters different: each gamete is a different draw of one chromosome from every pair.

props.caption: How much of your DNA each ancestor contributed

visual.alt: Three bars to scale: fifty per cent of your DNA from a parent, twenty-five per cent from a grandparent and twelve and a half per cent from a great-grandparent

examples.title: Identical twins
examples.body: Two people with exactly the same DNA are the best experiment nature runs. Identical twins come from one fertilised egg that split, so they share every allele, and they have the same blood group, the same eye colour and faces that fool their friends. They still differ, in height by a little, in weight often by a lot, in fingerprints, scars, accents and skills. Every one of those differences is the environment at work on the same genes. It is the clearest evidence that what you inherit is a range, and life decides where in it you land.

boxes.title: Always the same
boxes.body: Blood group, eye colour: inherited only.

boxes.title: Often different
boxes.body: Weight, fitness, skills: genes plus environment.

boxes.title: The lesson
boxes.body: Genes set the range; the environment picks the point.

visual.alt: Four boxes round the title Same genes, different people: inherited-only features twins share, features that depend on genes and environment, features that are environmental only, and the lesson that genes set a range

examples.title: The blood-group chart on the hospital wall
examples.body: A hospital needs to know which blood it can give to whom, and blood group is the cleanest example of a characteristic that comes in boxes. You are O, A, B or AB and nothing in between, because one gene decides it. Count a class and you get a bar chart with gaps, most people in O and A, a few in B and AB. Measure the same class's height and you get the opposite picture: a smooth spread with a peak in the middle, because hundreds of genes and years of meals all contribute a little.

steps.title: Nested boxes: cell, nucleus, chromosome, DNA, gene
steps.body:
Every instruction for building and running you is stored in your cells, and the storage is a set of boxes inside boxes.

- Almost every **cell** has a **nucleus**.
- The nucleus holds **chromosomes**: in a human body cell, **46** of them, arranged as **23 pairs**. One chromosome of each pair came from your mother and one from your father.
- Each chromosome is one very long, tightly coiled molecule of **DNA**.
- A **gene** is a short section of that DNA that carries the instruction for **one characteristic**, by telling the cell how to build one **protein**. Humans have about **20 000** genes, spread along the 46 chromosomes.

So the order, from big to small, is **cell, nucleus, chromosome, DNA, gene**, and questions test whether you have it the right way round. A gene is *part of* a chromosome, not the other way about.

**Why 23 pairs matters.** You have two copies of every chromosome, so you have two copies of every gene, one from each parent. The two copies may be the same or slightly different versions. That is where inheritance starts, and the GCSE Genetics unit spends a whole topic on it.

**The same DNA in every cell.** A skin cell and a nerve cell carry the same 46 chromosomes; they differ because they use different genes. The full set of instructions travels with every cell.

visuals.alt: A flow chart from big to small: a cell holds a nucleus, the nucleus holds forty-six chromosomes in twenty-three pairs, each chromosome is one long molecule of DNA, and a gene is a section of it coding for one protein

check.prompt: How many chromosomes are there in the nucleus of a human body cell?
check.solution: **46**, arranged as **23 pairs**: one chromosome of each pair from each parent.

steps.title: The double helix and its four letters
steps.body:
DNA is a molecule shaped like a **twisted ladder**: two long strands wound round each other in a **double helix**. The rungs of the ladder are pairs of **bases**, and there are only four kinds, written by their initials: **A, T, C and G**.

**The bases pair in a fixed way.** **A always pairs with T**, and **C always pairs with G**. So if you know one strand, you know the other: opposite every A there is a T, opposite every C a G. That rule is called **complementary base pairing**, and it is why DNA can be **copied**. When a cell divides, the two strands are separated and each is used as a template to build a new partner, so both new cells get the full code.

**The order of the bases is the code.** Along one strand the bases read like a sentence, ATGCCGTA and so on, and it is that order that spells out the instructions. A gene is one stretch of that sentence. Change a letter and you may change the instruction: that is a **mutation**.

**A consequence you can calculate.** Because A pairs with T, the amount of A in any DNA sample equals the amount of T, and C equals G. If a sample is 30% A, it is 30% T, and the remaining 40% is split equally: 20% C and 20% G.

props.title: Know one strand and you know the other

visuals.alt: A table of the four DNA bases and their partners: adenine with thymine, cytosine with guanine

visuals.problem: A sample of DNA is 30% A. What percentage is T, C and G?

steps.text: A pairs with T, so T = A = 30%
A and T together: 30 + 30 = 60%, leaving 100 − 60 = 40% for C and G
C pairs with G, so they share the 40% equally: C = 20%, G = 20%

check.prompt: A DNA sample is 20% G. What percentage of its bases are C?
check.solution: C pairs with G, so the amounts are equal: **20%** C. (A and T then share the remaining 60%, 30% each.)

steps.title: Watson, Crick, Wilkins and Franklin
steps.body:
The shape of DNA was worked out in **1953**, and four people did it.

- **Rosalind Franklin** and **Maurice Wilkins**, at King's College London, fired **X-rays** through fibres of DNA and photographed the pattern the rays made. Franklin's photograph known as **Photo 51**, taken in **1952**, showed the cross-shaped pattern of a **helix** and gave its measurements.
- **James Watson** and **Francis Crick**, in Cambridge, built **models** from the measurements and the chemistry of the bases, and in 1953 produced the double helix with the bases pairing A to T and C to G.

**Why the pairing was the real prize.** The moment the model was built, it was obvious how DNA could be copied: split the strands and each is a template for its partner. Watson and Crick's paper made the point in one famous sentence.

**The credit.** The Nobel Prize for the discovery went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins in **1962**. Franklin had died in **1958**, and the prize is never given after death, so her X-ray work, which the model depended on, went unrecognised for years. Her name is now on the story as firmly as the other three, and the National Curriculum names all four.

The lesson about science is worth keeping: the discovery needed **two kinds of evidence**, the X-ray patterns and the model building, from two teams who did not always share.

steps.title: What a gene does
steps.body:
A gene is an instruction for making one **protein**, and proteins do the work of the cell: **enzymes** that run its reactions, **structural** proteins that build it, **pigments** that colour hair and eyes, **hormones** that carry messages. Your characteristics are the sum of the proteins your genes code for.

**Versions of a gene are alleles.** You have two copies of every gene, one on each chromosome of a pair. The copies can be different versions, called **alleles**: the gene for a pigment might come in a version that makes lots and a version that makes little. Which alleles you inherited decides which proteins you make, and so which characteristics you show. The GCSE unit on inheritance works out the rules.

**Not everything is in the genes.** Characteristics come in three kinds:

- **Inherited** only: blood group, eye colour, whether you can roll your tongue is often quoted but is not a clean example; blood group is.
- **Environmental** only: scars, an accent, a language you speak, a tan.
- **Both**: height, weight, skin colour, how good you are at a sport. Genes set a range; food, exercise and practice decide where in it you end up.

**Variation** is the name for the differences between individuals, and it has the same two sources: **genetic** variation from the alleles, and **environmental** variation from how life went. Identical twins share every allele and still differ, which is the proof that both matter.

props.title: Genes set a range; the environment decides where in it

visuals.alt: A table of characteristics sorted by whether they are inherited, environmental, or both: blood group and eye colour inherited, a scar and an accent environmental, height and weight both

check.prompt: Which of these characteristics is caused only by the environment?
check.solution: A **scar** comes from an injury, not from any gene. Blood group and eye colour are inherited; height is both, genes setting a range and food while growing deciding where in it.

A scar
Blood group

steps.title: Continuous and discontinuous variation
steps.body:
Variation comes in two shapes, and you can tell them apart from the chart.

**Discontinuous variation** has **distinct groups** and nothing in between. Blood group is O, A, B or AB; there is no AO-and-a-half. Sex is another. It is usually controlled by a **single gene** and shown on a **bar chart** with gaps between the bars.

**Continuous variation** can take **any value in a range**. Height, hand span, mass, the length of a leaf: measure precisely enough and no two people are the same. It is controlled by **many genes together**, and by the environment as well, and it is shown by grouping the measurements into equal ranges and drawing a **frequency chart**, one bar for each range. The chart is usually highest in the middle and lower at the ends.

**Measuring it in class.** Hand span is easy: stretch a hand on a ruler, thumb tip to little-finger tip, and record to the nearest millimetre. Group the results into equal ranges, count each range, and draw the chart. Thirty students give a decent shape; five do not.

**Reading the charts.** For a discontinuous characteristic, the useful figure is *which group is commonest*. For a continuous one, it is *the middle of the range*, and *how spread out* the values are.

steps.title: Sexual reproduction shuffles the code
steps.body:
**Gametes carry half.** A sperm cell and an egg cell each carry **23** chromosomes, one from each pair, not 46. At **fertilisation** the two sets join to make **46** again. That is why you have one of each pair from each parent, and why the number does not double every generation.

**Which 23?** When a gamete is made, it gets one chromosome from each pair, chosen at random. With 23 pairs there are millions of possible combinations, and each sperm and each egg is a different draw. So two children of the same parents get a different mix, and **brothers and sisters differ**. Sexual reproduction produces **variation** every time.

**Twins.** **Identical** twins come from **one** fertilised egg that splits into two embryos: they share every allele, and any differences between them are environmental. **Non-identical** twins come from **two** eggs fertilised by two sperm at the same time: they are as alike as any brother and sister.

**Asexual reproduction does not shuffle.** Bacteria splitting in two, a strawberry plant sending out runners, a potato sprouting from an old potato: one parent, no gametes, and offspring that are **genetically identical** to the parent, called **clones**. It is fast and needs no partner, but produces no variation, which matters when the environment changes.

props.title: Shuffling comes from gametes and fertilisation

visuals.alt: A table comparing sexual and asexual reproduction: two parents against one, gametes of twenty-three chromosomes against none, varied offspring against clones

check.prompt: How many chromosomes does a human sperm cell carry?
check.solution: **23**: one from each of the 23 pairs. The egg carries 23 as well, so fertilisation restores the **46** of a body cell.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Pairing is why DNA can be copied.** Because each base has one partner, one strand carries all the information needed to rebuild the other. Split the helix, add bases to each half, and two identical molecules result. That is the sentence Watson and Crick added at the end of their paper, and it turned a shape into a mechanism.

**A gene is an instruction, not a characteristic.** The gene codes for a protein; the characteristic follows from what the protein does. A change of one base in a gene can change the protein's shape, and a misshapen enzyme may not work at all. That is how a single mutation can cause a disease, and it is why the GCSE unit on protein synthesis exists.

**The same genes, different results.** Identical twins are the cleanest evidence that genes and environment both matter: same alleles, and yet different heights, weights, fingerprints and lives. When a question asks whether a characteristic is inherited or environmental, the strong answer often says *both, and here is how much of each*.

**Halves of halves.** You share half your DNA with each parent, a quarter with each grandparent, an eighth with each great-grandparent. An ancestry test that reports a quarter from one region is finding a grandparent, not a mystery.

**Continuous variation is many genes plus environment.** Height is set by hundreds of genes, each adding a little, and by nutrition while growing. That is why it forms a smooth spread with a peak in the middle rather than a few separate groups: many small contributions add up to a curve. Discontinuous variation is usually one gene, which is why it comes in a few boxes.

**Clones and risk.** A field of potatoes grown from cuttings is one genotype repeated. If a disease can kill one plant, it can kill the field, because there is no variation for it to fail against. Sexual reproduction is slower and needs a partner, but it produces the variation on which natural selection, the next topic, depends.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Cell → nucleus → chromosome → DNA → gene.** A human body cell has **46** chromosomes in **23 pairs**, one of each pair from each parent.
- A **gene** is a section of DNA coding for one **protein**, and so for one characteristic. About **20 000** genes in a human.
- DNA is a **double helix** with four bases: **A pairs with T, C pairs with G**. The **order** of bases is the code; the pairing lets DNA be **copied**.
- Base percentages: A = T and C = G, and the four sum to 100. 30% A means 30% T, 20% C, 20% G.
- **Franklin** and **Wilkins**: X-rays (Photo 51, 1952). **Watson** and **Crick**: the model, **1953**. Nobel Prize 1962; Franklin had died in 1958.
- Different versions of a gene are **alleles**. Characteristics are **inherited**, **environmental**, or **both**.
- **Discontinuous** variation: distinct groups, one gene, bar chart with gaps (blood group). **Continuous**: any value in a range, many genes plus environment, frequency chart (height).
- **Gametes** carry **23** chromosomes; fertilisation restores 46 and mixes the parents' alleles, so siblings differ. **Identical twins** come from one egg; **clones** from asexual reproduction have no variation.

questions.prompt: Why does complementary base pairing allow DNA to be copied?
questions.solution: Because A pairs only with T and C only with G, one strand fixes the other. Separate the strands, build a new partner on each, and two identical molecules result. That copying happens before every cell division.

questions.solution: A pairs with T, so the amounts are equal: **24%** A. The other 52% is C and G, 26% each.

questions.prompt: What name is given to a different version of the same gene?
questions.solution: An **allele**. You have two copies of each gene, one on each chromosome of a pair, and the copies may be different alleles: for example a version of a pigment gene that makes more, and one that makes less.

questions.solution: A gamete carries **one chromosome from each pair, chosen at random**, so each sperm and each egg is a different draw. Two children are two different draws from the same parents. All human DNA uses the same four bases.

questions.prompt: Put these in order from largest to smallest.
questions.solution: The **cell** contains the **nucleus**, which contains the **chromosomes**, and a **gene** is a section of the DNA of one chromosome. Big to small: cell, nucleus, chromosome, gene.

questions.prompt: A sample of DNA is 24% T. What percentage of its bases are G?
questions.solution: T = A = 24%, so A and T together are 48%. The remaining $100 - 48 = 52\%$ is C and G in equal amounts: **26%** G.

questions.solution: Height shows **continuous** variation, controlled by **many genes** and by the **environment**. The genes set what is possible; nutrition while growing decides how much of it happens. Identical twins with the same genes can end up different heights.

questions.prompt: A mutation changes one base in a gene that codes for an enzyme. Why might this stop the enzyme working?
questions.solution: A gene's base order decides the **protein** built from it. Change a base and the protein may be built differently, and an enzyme works by **shape**: its active site must fit its substrate. A changed shape may fit nothing, and the reaction it ran stops.

questions.prompt: Describe how genetic information is stored in a cell, from the nucleus down to the bases, and explain how the structure of DNA allows it to be copied and to carry instructions.
questions.solution:
Genetic information is stored in boxes inside boxes. The **nucleus** of a cell holds the **chromosomes**: in a human body cell there are **46**, arranged as **23 pairs**, with one of each pair inherited from each parent. Each chromosome is a single very long, tightly coiled molecule of **DNA**. A **gene** is a short section of that DNA, and each gene carries the instruction for one **protein**. Humans have about 20 000 genes spread along the 46 chromosomes, and every body cell carries the full set.

DNA is shaped as a **double helix**: two strands twisted round each other like a ladder. The rungs are pairs of **bases**, of which there are four, **A, T, C and G**. The pairing is fixed: **A always pairs with T**, and **C always pairs with G**. This is complementary base pairing, and it means that if you know the order of bases on one strand, you know the order on the other, because every A faces a T and every C faces a G.

That is what lets DNA be **copied**. Before a cell divides, the two strands are separated, and each strand is used as a **template**: free bases pair up with the exposed bases, T against A and G against C, until each old strand has a new partner. The result is two identical double helices, one for each new cell. Watson and Crick saw this at once when they built the model in 1953, from the X-ray evidence of Franklin and Wilkins.

The **order** of the bases is the **code**. Along a gene the sequence of A, T, C and G is read by the cell as the instruction for building one protein, and proteins, as enzymes, structures and pigments, produce the characteristics. If one base is changed, a **mutation**, the protein may be built differently; an enzyme with the wrong shape may not work, which is how a single changed letter can change a characteristic or cause a disease.

Describes DNA as a double helix of two strands with bases A, T, C and G, paired A with T and C with G.
Explains copying: complementary pairing means each strand is a template for the other, so the strands separate and each rebuilds its partner.
Explains the code: the order of bases in a gene is the instruction for one protein, and a changed base is a mutation that can change the protein.

questions.modelAnswer:
Genetic information is stored in boxes inside boxes. The **nucleus** of a cell holds the **chromosomes**: in a human body cell there are **46**, arranged as **23 pairs**, with one of each pair inherited from each parent. Each chromosome is a single very long, tightly coiled molecule of **DNA**. A **gene** is a short section of that DNA, and each gene carries the instruction for one **protein**. Humans have about 20 000 genes spread along the 46 chromosomes, and every body cell carries the full set.

DNA is shaped as a **double helix**: two strands twisted round each other like a ladder. The rungs are pairs of **bases**, of which there are four, **A, T, C and G**. The pairing is fixed: **A always pairs with T**, and **C always pairs with G**. This is complementary base pairing, and it means that if you know the order of bases on one strand, you know the order on the other, because every A faces a T and every C faces a G.

That is what lets DNA be **copied**. Before a cell divides, the two strands are separated, and each strand is used as a **template**: free bases pair up with the exposed bases, T against A and G against C, until each old strand has a new partner. The result is two identical double helices, one for each new cell. Watson and Crick saw this at once when they built the model in 1953, from the X-ray evidence of Franklin and Wilkins.

The **order** of the bases is the **code**. Along a gene the sequence of A, T, C and G is read by the cell as the instruction for building one protein, and proteins, as enzymes, structures and pigments, produce the characteristics. If one base is changed, a **mutation**, the protein may be built differently; an enzyme with the wrong shape may not work, which is how a single changed letter can change a characteristic or cause a disease.

questions.prompt: A newspaper says "identical twins are exactly the same in every way". Evaluate this claim, using what you know about genes, environment and variation.
questions.solution:
The claim is right about the genes and wrong about everything built on them. **Identical twins** come from **one egg** fertilised by one sperm, which then splits into two embryos. Both embryos carry the same 46 chromosomes and the **same alleles** of every gene, which is why identical twins have the same blood group, the same eye colour and faces that are hard to tell apart. Everything that is **inherited only** really is identical between them.

But a characteristic is not the same thing as a gene. Genes code for proteins, and what the body does with those proteins depends on what happens to it. Some characteristics are **environmental only**: a scar, a broken nose, an accent picked up from friends, a language learned. Twins can differ in all of these from the day they are born. Others are **both**: height, weight, fitness, skill at an instrument. Genes set a range, and food, exercise and practice decide where in the range each twin ends up. Even **fingerprints** differ, because the ridges form partly by chance in the womb. A twin who eats better, trains harder or practises longer will be taller, stronger or more skilled than the other, with exactly the same DNA.

That is why twins matter to biologists. Two people with the same alleles who still differ are the cleanest evidence that **variation** has two sources, genetic and environmental, and that continuous characteristics like height are not fixed by inheritance alone. If genes decided everything, identical twins would be interchangeable, and they are not.

So the fair version of the headline is: identical twins are **genetically identical**, and different in every way that the world has had a hand in. The distinction matters because the same is true of everyone: what you inherit is a starting point, not a verdict.

criteria.text: Explains that identical twins come from one fertilised egg that splits, so they share every allele, which is why they look so alike and have the same blood group and eye colour.
Explains that characteristics are inherited, environmental or both, with examples of environmental differences twins can have: scars, accents, weight, fingerprints, skills.
Uses the twins as evidence that continuous characteristics such as height depend on the environment as well as genes.
Reaches a judgement: identical in their genes, not in every way, and says why the distinction matters.

examTechnique.body:
This topic is tested by **definitions in the right order** and **one small calculation**. The order is cell, nucleus, chromosome, DNA, gene, and a question that gives you the words jumbled is checking exactly that. The calculation is base percentages: partner equals partner, the four add to 100.

*Explain* questions want the mechanism behind the fact. Not *DNA can be copied* but *because A pairs only with T and C only with G, each strand is a template for the other*. Not *siblings differ* but *because each gamete carries a random one of each chromosome pair*. For variation, name the kind, say what controls it, and name the chart.
examinerErrors: Putting a gene **above** a chromosome in the order. A gene is a **section of** a chromosome's DNA.
Giving a gamete **46** chromosomes, or a body cell **23**.
Pairing A with C or A with G. It is **A with T** and **C with G**.
Forgetting that the four bases add to **100%** when working out percentages.
Saying a gene *is* a characteristic. A gene codes for a **protein**; the characteristic follows.
Drawing continuous data as a few named categories instead of grouping it into ranges, or calling blood group continuous.
Crediting the DNA model to Franklin, or the X-ray photographs to Watson and Crick. **X-rays in London, model in Cambridge.**
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats the structure of DNA as a **mechanism**: base pairing is why it can be copied, the order of bases is why it can carry instructions, and one changed base is why a mutation can change a protein. It gets the levels in order without thinking, works the base percentages in two lines and checks that they add to 100. On variation it names the kind, the cause and the chart, and for anything continuous it says *many genes and the environment*. Given twins, it uses them as evidence rather than an example. And it tells the history straight: Franklin's X-rays in 1952, the model in 1953, a prize in 1962 that could not include a scientist who died in 1958.
